# The Forcing Function — Agency Choices & Recommendations {.unnumbered}

The question is no longer *whether* the SQL Server estate changes. Microsoft is
moving the identity floor underneath it — retiring the protocols and versions the
estate was built on — on a timeline the agency does not set. This page is the
decision layer over the eleven-book series: it names the pressures forcing the
change, separates **what is forced** from **what is a choice**, lays the three
destinations side by side, and maps an agency profile to a recommended path.

It is deliberately neutral. There is no universal winner — only a destination
that fits a given estate, licensing position, and operating model. The reasoning
behind each cell lives in the books; this page names the decision.

::: {.callout-important appearance="default"}
## Status — Draft
This brief is **DRAFT v0.1**, the decision companion to **Book 11** and to
**ADR-091** (SQL Server Engine Authentication Transformation, **PROPOSED**). The
external facts it cites — version lifecycle dates, Extended Security Update
terms, and the NTLM deprecation timeline — are Microsoft program facts that shift;
**verify each against the Microsoft Lifecycle and "Extended Security Updates
enabled by Azure Arc" documentation before committing a date to a plan.** Treat
the recommendation matrix as analytical, not normative, until ADR-091 is accepted.
:::

## Why now — the three forcing functions

Three independent pressures are converging. None of them, on its own, is a
flag-day switch; together they make "stay fully on-premises, Active-Directory-
anchored, never touch Arc, keep Windows Authentication" progressively untenable
rather than impossible.

| # | Forcing function | What it is | What it forces |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Version end-of-support** | Each SQL Server version carries roughly five years of mainstream + five years of extended support (~10 years), after which security updates stop. | A **version upgrade** — *not* Arc by itself. An out-of-support engine receives no patches and becomes an audit and ATO liability. |
| **2** | **ESU gated behind Azure Arc** | Past end-of-support, Extended Security Updates (ESU) keep critical patches flowing. The streamlined, pay-as-you-go ESU path is **delivered and billed through Azure Arc**; ESUs are offered free for instances migrated to / enabled by Azure. | **Arc enablement** as the practical price of staying patched on an out-of-support version. A traditional volume-license ESU path still exists without Arc, but it is the harder, time-boxed option. |
| **3** | **NTLM deprecation** | Microsoft is actively deprecating NTLM and hardening defaults toward Kerberos. SQL Server's silent NTLM fallback (Book 01) breaks when NTLM is blocked network-wide, and the block does not distinguish excepted instances from the rest. (ADR-068) | A move **off Windows Authentication's NTLM fallback** toward Kerberos and ultimately Microsoft Entra token authentication — independent of version or Arc. |

::: {.callout-note}
These three are not one decision. Version end-of-support forces a *version*
move; ESU-via-Arc forces *Arc enablement* if you stay on an out-of-support
version; NTLM deprecation forces an *authentication* move. An estate can be hit
by all three at once, on different instances, on different clocks.
:::

## What is forced — and what is a choice

The single most important distinction on this page. Conflating the two is what
makes the program feel like a Microsoft mandate with no agency. It is not.

::: {.callout-important title="Forced vs. chosen"}
**Forced (the floor moves regardless of what you decide):**

- Move **off NTLM** and off Windows Authentication's silent NTLM fallback.
- Move **off end-of-support engine versions** — patch or leave the version.
- If you stay on an out-of-support version, **Arc enablement** becomes the
  practical path to keep receiving Extended Security Updates.

**Chosen (yours to decide, and the subject of the matrix below):**

- **Where you land** — stay on SQL Server, or consolidate onto PostgreSQL or
  Oracle.
- **How far you consolidate** — re-authenticate the silos in place, or dissolve
  them toward a single authoritative database (the SSOT goal of Book 11).
- **Your timeline within the forced windows** — which instances move first.
:::

The forced part is an **authentication-layer** change; the chosen part is a
**platform-layer** change. They are sequenced, not simultaneous — and the
authentication work comes first regardless of the destination, because it is
what produces the rationalized estate inventory that scopes any platform move
(Book 03, Book 11 Chapter 1).

## Your three destinations

Every retained instance ends up at one of three destinations. All three satisfy
the *forced* requirement — auth that is observable and conditionable in the
identity plane. They differ in effort, licensing, and how far they advance the
SSOT goal.

| Dimension | **A · Stay on SQL Server** | **B · Consolidate to PostgreSQL** | **C · Consolidate to Oracle** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | SQL Server 2022, Arc-enabled, Windows Auth → Microsoft Entra token auth | Re-platform onto PostgreSQL (Crunchy Data on Red Hat OpenShift / ROSA GovCloud, RDS/Aurora, or Azure DB for PostgreSQL) | Re-platform onto Oracle (19c on OpenShift Virtualization, or Autonomous DB in OCI US Gov Cloud) |
| **Auth model** | Entra OAuth 2.0 token (`FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER`), Conditional Access | Entra-native on Azure DB for PostgreSQL; OrgPath roles + Row-Level Security elsewhere | Oracle auth integrated to the chosen identity plane |
| **Engine effort** | **Low** — upgrade to 2022, Arc-enable, migrate logins (Books 03–06) | **High** — schema + T-SQL→PL/pgSQL conversion (SSMA / AWS SCT+DMS), app changes (Red Hat MTA) | **High** — T-SQL→PL/SQL conversion (Oracle SQL Developer), app changes (MTA) |
| **Licensing** | Continues SQL Server per-core licensing | **Eliminates** SQL Server licensing; open-source + commercial support (Crunchy/EDB) | Oracle licensing — low incremental cost **only if** an Oracle site license already exists |
| **FedRAMP path** | GCC-Moderate (Entra) / Arc | RDS, Aurora, **Crunchy on ROSA GovCloud**, Azure DB for PostgreSQL | **OCI US Gov Cloud (FedRAMP High)**, OpenShift Virtualization |
| **SSOT advance** | None — re-authenticates the silos, does not dissolve them | **High** — logical replication, RLS, JSONB, FDW toward one authoritative DB | **High** — consolidation onto an existing Oracle authority |
| **Best fit when** | Sprawl is low; timeline is tight; SQL-specific features in use | OpenShift-first; no significant Oracle estate; licensing exit is a goal | Significant existing Oracle estate; heavy PL/SQL corpus; Oracle-credentialed DBAs |

::: {.callout-tip}
Destinations B and C are not a way to *escape* the forced authentication work —
they **relocate** it. You still do the Book 03 audit and rationalization first;
the re-platform is what you do with the instances you choose not to retain on
SQL Server.
:::

## The recommendation matrix

There is no universal recommendation — the right destination is a function of the
estate. Read down to the first profile that matches; the criteria are drawn from
Book 11 Chapters 2 and 3.

| If the agency profile is… | Recommended destination | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Low instance count, well-configured Windows Auth, **tight timeline**, SQL-specific features in use | **A · Stay on SQL Server 2022 + Entra** | The forced work (upgrade, Arc, Entra logins) is the whole job; re-platform cost is not justified by the sprawl. |
| **OpenShift-first** footprint (ROSA GovCloud), **no significant Oracle** estate, licensing exit is a stated goal, CRUD-heavy workloads | **B · PostgreSQL** | Crunchy on ROSA aligns DB ops with the existing OpenShift model; eliminates per-core licensing; mature SSMA/SCT/DMS toolchain. |
| **Significant existing Oracle** estate, **large/complex PL/SQL** corpus, Oracle-credentialed DBA team, Oracle site license already paid | **C · Oracle** | Consolidating onto Oracle *reduces* platform count; adding PostgreSQL alongside Oracle would *add* one. PL/SQL + DBA continuity favor Oracle. |
| **High sprawl** (dozens of overlapping instances), SSOT consolidation is the explicit goal, mixed/uncertain Oracle position | **B · PostgreSQL (default re-platform)** | PostgreSQL's logical replication, RLS, JSONB, FDW, and schema-tenancy are the SSOT consolidation primitives; the toolchain is the most mature. Evaluate C only if an Oracle estate already exists. |
| Database must remain **co-located with Azure** workloads (data sovereignty / network topology) | **A** or **B via Azure DB for PostgreSQL** | Keeps the data inside the Microsoft GCC-Moderate boundary while still meeting the consolidation goal. |

::: {.callout-note}
**Two estates, two answers is normal.** The matrix applies per data domain, not
per agency. A realistic outcome is a *blend*: retain a handful of SQL Server 2022
instances on Entra (A) for SQL-specific workloads, consolidate the long tail onto
PostgreSQL (B), and fold Oracle-adjacent data into the existing Oracle estate (C).
The goal is fewer authoritative platforms — not a single vendor.
:::

## Decision sequence

1. **Audit & rationalize first** (Book 02–03). Inventory every instance, surface
   silent NTLM fallback, and classify each instance retire / consolidate / retain.
   This is forced work and it produces the inventory every later choice depends on.
2. **Do the forced authentication move** on the retain set (Books 04–06): Arc-
   enable, stand up Entra logins alongside Windows logins, cut over, retire the
   old logins. The two auth modes coexist during the parallel run.
3. **Then make the platform choice** per data domain using the matrix above.
   Re-platform (B/C) follows the same parallel-run discipline — establish the
   target, validate in parallel, cut over only after the validation window.
   *Never drop before you observe.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Division of labor"}
**Microsoft and the platform vendors provide:** the Entra authentication plane and
Arc Managed Identity that satisfy the forced requirement; the rationalization tools
(Azure Migrate, DMA, Defender for SQL); the migration toolchains (SSMA, AWS SCT+DMS,
Oracle SQL Developer, Red Hat MTA); and the FedRAMP-authorized hosting targets.

**What only you can provide:** the data-authority decision — which instance is
authoritative for each domain; the application and PL/SQL inventory that decides
whether a workload can re-platform cheaply or must be retained; the licensing and
DBA-skills assessment that picks B vs. C; and the program sequencing that stays
ahead of Microsoft's version, ESU, and NTLM clocks.
:::
